title: Project Northstar automated dependency-update merging
question: Should Project Northstar enable automatic merging for AI-generated dependency updates during the next four-week release cycle?
verdict: Do not enable automatic merging under the currently proposed rule for the next four-week release cycle. The observed low-risk replay supports investigating a narrower rule, but it does not cover the high-risk surfaces that the proposal still includes, and rollback readiness and recommendation provenance remain unresolved.

nodes.label: Current position
nodes.text: Do not enable automatic merging under the current proposed rule during the next release cycle.

nodes.label: The current rule includes untested high-risk updates
nodes.text: Because the proposal excludes neither install-script packages nor authentication-directory updates, it includes update classes outside the controlled replay.

nodes.label: Rollback readiness is not demonstrated
nodes.text: The fixture provides no recorded rollback drill or recovery-time measurement for a bad automatically merged dependency update.

nodes.label: Automation could reduce a material review delay
nodes.text: Routine patch-update review had a 31-hour median wait in the previous four-week cycle.

nodes.label: Required checks performed well for the tested low-risk replay
nodes.text: In the controlled replay, 18 of 20 low-risk patch updates passed without manual edits and both failures were caught before merge.

nodes.label: Recommendation provenance cannot be verified
nodes.text: It is unknown which model, prompt, or retrieved advisory produced a generated pull-request recommendation, because no signed provenance record exists. This could change whether such recommendations are acceptable inputs to automatic merging.

nodes.label: Required-check coverage for included risk classes is unknown
nodes.text: It is unknown whether the required checks detect harmful updates involving install scripts, authentication and authorization code, or major versions; those classes were absent from the replay but remain in the proposed rule.

nodes.label: Controlled replay passed most tested updates
nodes.text: The synthetic replay reports 18 of 20 low-risk patch updates passing the complete test suite without manual edits, with both failures detected before merge.

nodes.label: Replay excludes several risk classes
nodes.text: The replay did not include major-version updates, packages with install scripts, or changes modifying authentication and authorization code.

nodes.label: Generated-description provenance is absent
nodes.text: The fixture has no signed provenance record for generated pull-request descriptions, so a reviewer cannot verify the model, prompt, or retrieved advisory from the description alone.

nodes.label: Current proposal lacks high-risk exclusions
nodes.text: The proposed rule excludes neither packages with install scripts nor updates touching the authentication directory.

nodes.label: Patch updates wait for review
nodes.text: The synthetic team recorded a 31-hour median wait for routine patch-update review during the previous four-week cycle.

nodes.label: No rollback drill is recorded
nodes.text: No rollback drill has been recorded for an automatically merged dependency update, and the fixture has no recovery-time measurement after a bad merge.

edges.note: A rule that includes update classes absent from the successful replay gives reason not to enable it as currently scoped.
Without demonstrated rollback and recovery readiness, the consequence of a bad automatic merge is not bounded for this release cycle.
A 31-hour routine-review delay is a practical reason to favor automation, weighing against a decision not to enable it.
Successful checks on the tested low-risk patches are evidence for an automated path, weighing against a blanket no-enable decision.
Verifiable recommendation provenance is missing; resolving it could change whether AI-generated recommendations can safely trigger automatic merging.
Evidence that required checks cover the risk classes still included in the proposal is missing and could change the provisional decision.
The replay’s pass and pre-merge detection results support the claim that required checks performed well for its tested low-risk patch updates.
The omitted major, install-script, and authentication/authorization changes establish that coverage for those classes was not observed in the replay.
The replay result applies only to low-risk patch updates because the cited higher-risk classes were not included.
The absence of a signed provenance record supports the stated unknown about tracing generated recommendations.
The proposal’s lack of exclusions supports the claim that it includes install-script and authentication-directory updates outside the replay.
The recorded 31-hour median review wait supports the claim that automation could relieve a material queue delay.
The lack of a recorded rollback drill and recovery-time measurement supports the claim that rollback readiness is not demonstrated.
